passage:
"I'm not going to the police," said Manoj. "They'll ask why I was out at night and say it was my fault."
"Your phone was taken at the bus stop at nine," said Gautam. "You were coming from tuition. Why would that be your fault?"
"They'll make me run around for weeks."
"Then let's write everything now. Time, place, what he looked like, the phone's details. I'll come with you."
At the station the duty officer said, "Sit. Tell me slowly." She wrote it all, read it back, and gave Manoj a copy with a number.
Outside, Manoj exhaled. "I thought it would be worse."
"If they had refused, we would have gone to the senior officer," said Gautam. "Or asked legal aid."
"Fine. But thanks for coming."

qa.q: What did Manoj and Gautam write down before going to the station?
qa.a: They wrote the time, place, what he looked like and the phone's details.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling before he agreed to go to the police?
qa.a: Manoj felt afraid of being blamed and of running around for weeks, and hesitated to file the complaint.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that made the complaint easier?
qa.a: Gautam went with Manoj, helped write every detail beforehand and named the senior officer and legal aid as options if the police refused.

qa.q: How did the duty officer respond to Manoj's complaint?
qa.a: The duty officer asked Manoj to tell it slowly, wrote it all, read it back and gave a copy with a number, so the complaint was taken seriously.

grounding: A young adult hesitates to file a police complaint over theft, and going with a trusted person and writing details help.

passage:
For two weeks a man had waited by the lab gate and made comments as I passed. I told nobody. I was sure someone would ask what I was doing there so late, or tell me to ignore it. I began taking a longer route, and my stomach hurt every afternoon.
Tarun, a classmate, noticed my new route and asked. Something in me gave way and I told him. "Let's write down what happened. Dates, the place, what he said," Tarun suggested. "I'll come with you."
At the station the officer at the desk read what I had written, asked a few gentle questions, registered it and gave me a copy. I walked out still nervous, but lighter. I have taken the short route since.
Nazia

qa.q: What did the man do by the lab gate?
qa.a: He waited by the lab gate and made comments as Nazia passed.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling during the two weeks of silence?
qa.a: Nazia felt afraid and ashamed of being blamed, so told nobody and took a longer route, with a stomach that hurt every afternoon.

qa.q: What made it possible for Nazia to file the complaint?
qa.a: Tarun asked, listened, suggested writing down the dates, place and words, and went with Nazia to the station.

qa.q: How did the officer at the desk handle Nazia's complaint?
qa.a: The officer read Nazia's notes, asked a few gentle questions, registered the complaint and gave a copy, so Nazia left lighter.

grounding: A young adult hesitates to file a police complaint over harassment, and going with a trusted person and writing details helps.

passage:
Chetan's phone was snatched outside the metro station in Hyderabad. He stood there, stunned, then walked home without doing anything.
"Aren't you going to file a complaint?" his roommate Darshan asked.
"What's the point? They'll make me wait for hours, ask why I was careless, and nothing will happen."
Darshan sat down beside him. "Maybe. But you need the report to block the SIM and for insurance. Let's write everything down first: time, place, what he looked like, the phone's number and IMEI."
They made a list. Then Darshan went with him to the police station. The first constable said to come back tomorrow. Darshan politely asked to speak to the duty officer, who took the complaint and gave them a copy.
Walking back, Chetan said, "I really thought they'd blame me." Darshan shrugged. "Some might. That's why you take someone along."

qa.q: Where was Chetan's phone snatched?
qa.a: Outside the metro station in Hyderabad.

qa.q: Why did Chetan not want to file a complaint?
qa.a: Chetan felt fearful and hopeless, expecting long waits, blame for being careless and no result.

qa.q: What steps helped Chetan file the complaint?
qa.a: Writing down all the details, going with Darshan, and politely asking for the duty officer when the constable refused.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Chetan's reluctance?
qa.a: Darshan understands the fear but sees that the report is needed, so he stays calm and practical, offering to go along.

grounding: A young adult hesitates to file a police complaint about theft, expecting blame and delay, and a friend helps him write details and escalate politely.

passage:
"Ankita, you're shaking. What happened?"
"It's that guy from my old college, Mahima. He's made fake profiles with my photos. He's sending messages to my friends saying I'm his girlfriend."
"That's harassment. You need to report it."
"To the police? They'll ask what photos I posted. They'll say I brought it on myself."
"You didn't bring anything on yourself. He did this."
"What if they don't listen?"
"Then we go to the cyber cell, and if they refuse, we ask for the senior officer. And we'll call the women's helpline first, now, so you're not alone."
"Now?"
"Now. Take screenshots of everything: the profiles, the messages, the dates."
"Will you come?"
"Of course. And let's call your mother on the way. You shouldn't carry this alone."
Ankita wiped her face. "Okay. Okay."

qa.q: What had the man from Ankita's old college done?
qa.a: He made fake profiles with her photos and was sending messages to her friends.

qa.q: What is Ankita afraid of?
qa.a: Ankita is afraid that the police will blame her for the photos she posted and that they won't listen.

qa.q: What steps does Mahima suggest, and why are they valid?
qa.a: Mahima suggests screenshots, calling the women's helpline right away, going to the cyber cell, asking for a senior officer if refused, and telling Ankita's mother, so Ankita is supported.

qa.q: How might Ankita's mother feel when she's told?
qa.a: Her mother would likely feel worried and angry for her daughter, but glad Ankita told her.

grounding: A young adult hesitates to report online harassment, expecting blame, and a friend helps her record details and seek help the same day.

passage:
Two years ago, a man snatched my bag on my way home from college in Lucknow. My laptop, my ID, my notes, gone. I'm Deepika, and I didn't want to go to the police. I was sure they'd say, "Why were you walking alone so late?"
My friend Divyansh said, "We're going. Together. Now."
At the station, the first officer said, "Come tomorrow. It's late." I wanted to leave. Divyansh said politely, "Sir, could we speak to the SHO?" We waited forty minutes. The SHO took the complaint and gave me a copy.
Later, when nothing happened for a month, I wrote to the district legal aid office, with the complaint number. The investigating officer called me the following week.
The bag never came back. But the complaint helped me get a new ID, and it made me braver. Looking back, the fear of blame was worse than the station itself.

qa.q: What was in Deepika's bag?
qa.a: Deepika's laptop, ID and notes were in it.

qa.q: What was Deepika afraid of before going to the police?
qa.a: Deepika was afraid of being blamed, sure they would ask about walking alone so late.

qa.q: What steps helped Deepika's complaint go forward?
qa.a: Going with Divyansh, politely asking for the SHO when refused, keeping a copy, and writing to the legal aid office when nothing happened.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt at the station?
qa.a: Divyansh seemed calm and determined, wanting to support Deepika and make sure the complaint was filed.

grounding: A young adult who fears blame hesitates to report a theft, and going with a trusted friend, asking for a senior officer and seeking legal aid help.

passage:
Warden's note, Monday. Shalini Iyer, girls' hostel.
Sarita (Room 14) told me at 7 pm that her laptop and her grandmother's gold chain were stolen from her locked room on Saturday. She had not gone to the police. "They'll make me come ten times, and they'll ask why I left it there." She was close to tears; the laptop holds her final-year project.
What I did: we sat and wrote the details down together: the time she left, the time she returned, the broken latch, a description of the chain, the laptop's serial number from its box. At 8 pm I went with her to the police station. The duty officer first said, "Come tomorrow." I politely asked for the senior officer on duty. The complaint was registered by 9:15, and she has a copy. If anything stalls, the college legal aid cell meets on Wednesdays.

qa.q: By what time was the complaint registered?
qa.a: The complaint was registered by 9:15.

qa.q: Why hadn't Sarita gone to the police?
qa.a: Sarita was anxious about endless visits and afraid of being blamed for leaving things in the room, and was close to tears about the project.

qa.q: Which steps helped get the complaint registered?
qa.a: Writing the details down first, going with a trusted person, and politely asking for the senior officer when told to come tomorrow.

qa.q: How does the warden seem to see Sarita's fear of going?
qa.a: The warden treats it as understandable rather than foolish, and answers it by going along the same evening instead of just giving advice.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who hesitates to report a theft, expecting delay or blame, and how going with a trusted person, writing details and asking for a senior officer help.
